toc.title: Stage two: build your safety state
Stage three: mindfully experience your stuck defensive state

sections.title: Not about making it go away

blocks.p: There are three essential stages to trauma recovery. Here's what they are, and why I recommend them. No matter what path you're on, I think these three stages can help you map out your own trauma recovery: flesh out what you could do better, what's not going well, or what your next steps might be. They're also how I conceptualize the trauma recovery process as a therapist.

ol: Build your safety state and your vagal brake.

blocks.p: The first stage of trauma recovery is to equip yourself with really clear, accurate, precise foundational knowledge. Knowledge is power. This is where things start in your trauma recovery process.

Otherwise, you're going to be just following techniques and ideas and all these psychobabble psychological concepts that people throw out there. You'll be putting frozen peas on your chest to help yourself feel better. I saw that one recently. You'll be gargling, or dunking your head in water. You'll be chasing anything and everything that seems to be helpful, and maybe it is. Fine. But when you start with some solid foundational knowledge, it really puts you more in the driver's seat.

I recommend Polyvagal Theory as your go-to foundational knowledge piece. It's science. It's a good thing that it's falsifiable: it can be disproven. As of right now, it seems to be a pretty darn good explanation for trauma and how people get stuck in defensive states.

That's a lot different than going with some other belief system or psychological modality, like internal family systems, that requires you to first believe in something, like having multiple parts, like you have a firefighter inside of you. It's a lot different than thinking about yourself as ego and id and superego, or having a shadow, or whatever the hell else is popular right now. If you have to start from belief, maybe that's helpful, but I think there's a better way to go, and for me, Polyvagal Theory is the place to go.

It doesn't exclude everything else. There are people in my community who like the IFS stuff or the shadow stuff or whatever else. So it's not exclusionary, but in my opinion, it is unnecessary. I think attachment is a very compelling piece of foundational knowledge as well. But Polyvagal Theory is it for me.

Polyvagal Theory lays out some really core pieces of information, like the autonomic states and the polyvagal ladder. Basically, the way we respond to safety or danger is by shifting into different states our body can have: the safety state, where we can socially engage; the flight/fight state, where we can escape; or the shutdown state, where we collapse and maybe go numb or dissociate.
It's not that we choose these states. We shift in and out of them based on what we're neurocepting, which is a whole different concept from Polyvagal Theory, but connected.

When you learn these things, I think there's no judgment, and more validation and more understanding for yourself. If you can learn something like this and immediately reduce your shame and judgment and blame, that's going to set you up for a lot more success, I would argue.

blocks.h: Stage two: build your safety state

blocks.p: Once you've learned the polyvagal stuff, and hopefully gotten a new narrative for yourself with far less judgment and shame and self-blame, maybe even more compassion, the next step is to strengthen your safety state.

The basic idea is that there are biological pathways from your brainstem that are responsible for social engagement, or connection, when you're safe. The things you do like hugging others, smiling, making eye crinkles when you listen, those come from being in your safety state. Someone who's traumatized has less access to their safety state. So stage two is to develop your safety state more.

Safety is not just the literal environment. I'm not asking whether or not you're actually safe. Safety is a biological thing. It's about those specific biological pathways, the ventral vagal pathways.

When you strengthen those pathways, you also strengthen something called the vagal brake. The vagal brake is not a thing. It's more of a function of the safety state. If your safety state's strong enough, then as you get defensive activation like flight or fight, your vagal brake basically calms it down. It keeps your heartbeat at a calmer pace.

So the stronger your safety state, the stronger your vagal brake. The stronger your vagal brake, the less defensive activation you'll have, and the less hold your stuck, traumatized state will have over you. It will be less dominant.

You'll have more distress tolerance. If something in the environment would typically trigger you, it might still be triggering, but maybe less so, and over time much less so, and maybe even not at all at some point.

Part of this is that whatever trauma recovery journey you're on, maybe it involves journaling or meditating or therapy. Commonly, with these avenues, the trauma narrative might come up. I don't recommend you jump into it until you're ready, but it's normal for the details of the traumatic incidents or life circumstances to come up. If you're not ready for it, these things can be very dysregulating and even re-traumatizing. If your vagal brake is strong enough, you'll be able to tolerate the distress that comes along with these trauma narratives, if that's part of your recovery.

The way I work personally, I don't force this. I don't push or pressure my clients to talk about their trauma narrative. I don't think it's something they have to plow through and repeat over and over again until they're numb to it. I don't work that way.

I think things come up when they need to come up. That seems to be the case: if we can first feel safety, and then do the stage three work of actually feeling the defensive state, the narrative comes along with it as it needs to. And at that point they're able to share it, because their safety state is in a much stronger place.

Building your safety state and your vagal brake has a lot of other benefits too: more calmness, curiosity, confidence, and connection. All those really positive emotions and feelings and thoughts come along with the safety state. So the stronger your safety state is, the more of them you're going to have. Not just feelings, but sensations internally, thoughts, and connections with other people and with yourself.

Curiosity is one of those things, and that leads right to stage three. With more access to safety, you'll be more curious about the external world, and about what it's like to be you, in the external world and in your own internal world. Not just the happy stuff, but what else is inside of you. What is that stuck defensive state actually like?

You probably know what it's like when it's triggered and dysregulated and you're in a panic attack. But what about before that? What about when you're just moving through your day? You might have a moment to reflect and look inward and ask yourself, "What's it like to be me right now, in this moment?" That all comes from curiosity, and that curiosity comes from having more access to your safety state.
Deb Dana put it well when she was on the podcast:

q: When we begin to take away some of that judgment, that self-criticism, then there's room for curiosity. And curiosity is what you need in order to befriend.
blocks.cite: Deb Dana, [Deb Dana Interview: Story Follows State, Climbing the Ladder and Diagnosing (episode 29)](https://player.captivate.fm/episode/f8b9643c-28f8-4185-9525-8b4e6301516c)

blocks.h: Stage three: mindfully experience your stuck defensive state

blocks.p: The third stage of trauma healing is mindfully experiencing your stuck defensive state. This can be scary, I know. Hearing this might bring up, "Hell no, I'm not doing that." You might not be there yet, or ever, and that's fine.

By the way, "just" doing stage two brings a lot of benefits. You might say, "You know what? That's good enough. I'm feeling more connection. I'm feeling more calm. I'm feeling more confident, and I'm good. I don't want to go further into my stuck defensive state." That is completely an option. That's up to you and what you think is best for you.

But I do think taking things one step further as you're ready will naturally unfold, and it's also a choice you can make. Stage two alone may bring less dysregulation and more curiosity. But to really get unstuck and truly relieve your traumatic state to that next level, stage three, mindfully experiencing your stuck defensive state, is where that comes in.

That means actually allowing and experiencing whatever stuck state you have: flight, fight, shutdown, freeze. I don't think you ever really complete stage two. It's a constantly unfolding thing. But if you're entering stage three, your safety state is strong enough to welcome those stuck defensive states with curiosity. I know right now it might sound terrifying. But if you do stage two and build your vagal brake enough, there will be an impulse within you that says, "Hey, I'm ready to go further. I want to know what else is going on inside of me and what it's truly like to be me," without judgment, with welcoming and curiosity.

blocks.h3: Not about making it go away

blocks.p: The point of stage three is not to make your feelings and emotions and thoughts go away. That might sound weird, but it's not about making it go away. It's not about coping with it and managing your symptoms. Your presenting problems, like panic and anxiety, might reduce. I think that would be a natural result of this work, but it's not the goal.
The goal of stage three is to bring a gentle, nonjudgmental awareness to what it's like to be you, to whatever's happening inside of you. It's really about welcoming all of you, all of your feelings.

Sadly, I think this is what most therapists and most therapeutic modalities miss. In therapy school, we weren't taught the stage two stuff. We were told to jump to stage three, but stage three in therapy school is more about making things stop, making things go away.

What I'm saying is that after you build your safety state, stage three is about welcoming all of you: not just the safety, but also the defense. You welcome it with compassion and curiosity, and you're an observer to what is happening within you. Mindfulness is a really big part of this. As you mindfully allow your polyvagal defensive states, and all of you, a natural self-regulation process will unfold.
So self-regulation is not forced. Discharging your stuck trauma, or climbing your polyvagal ladder, is not forced. It's something that is allowed.
I have a method I call Allow to Witness to Experience. Very broadly:

ol: Allow your stuck defensive state to be present.

blocks.p: Again, stage three is about being with yourself, all of yourself, without judgment, without making it go away. The natural homeostatic self-regulation process will unfold on its own.

blocks.why: This article talks about mindfulness. This practice gives you a few minutes of it.

blocks.p: That's how I see trauma recovery, ladder climbing, and trauma discharging: three distinct phases one can go through. They overlap, yes, and each one builds upon the other. It's not quick. It's a long process.
